Designing complex time-to-event trials without simulation

Source: vignettes/DesignComplexSurvival.Rmd
DesignComplexSurvival.Rmd
library(DesignComplexSurvival)

DesignComplexSurvival computes the operating characteristics of two-group time-to-event trials analysed with the log-rank test, without patient-level simulation. Each group follows a four-state model (progression-free, progressed, switched, dead) with piecewise constant intensities. This vignette shows a single endpoint with a delayed treatment effect, then overall survival (OS) with treatment switching after progression, and finally progression-free survival (PFS) and OS tested together.

A delayed treatment effect

The control group has exponential survival with a median of 12 months. In the treatment group the hazard ratio is 1 for the first 6 months and 0.65 afterwards. Patients are enrolled at 10 per month for 3 months and at 30 per month afterwards, and the dropout hazard is 0.003 per month in both groups.

lam <- log(2) / 12
ctl <- ms_model(death = lam, dropout = 0.003)
trt <- ms_model(time = c(0, 6), death = c(lam, 0.65 * lam), dropout = 0.003)
acc <- ms_accrual(time = c(0, 3), rate = c(10, 30))
scn <- ms_scenario(ctl, trt, allocation = 1, accrual = acc)
ev <- ms_events(scn, n = 700, calendar_time = c(12, 24, 36))
ev[, c("time", "enrolled", "events_control", "events_treatment", "events")]
#>   time enrolled events_control events_treatment    events
#> 1   12      300       36.19604         34.58153  70.77756
#> 2   24      660      140.90234        124.55344 265.45579
#> 3   36      700      239.82054        206.40600 446.22654

With 700 patients, 446 events are expected by month 36.

The design has interim analyses at 50 and 75 percent of the events, an efficacy bound of O’Brien-Fleming type and a non-binding futility bound by beta spending. ms_size() finds the number of events for a power of 90 percent.

looks <- ms_looks("os", fraction = c(0.5, 0.75, 1))
test <- ms_test(futility = "beta", sf_fut = "HSD", param_fut = -2)
des <- ms_size(scn, looks = looks, test = test, power = 0.9,
               solve_for = "events", n = 700)
des
#> Solved for the final number of events: 587.802 (target power 0.9)
#> 
#> Group sequential log-rank design
#>   Tested endpoint: OS; looks driven by OS events
#>   Sample size: 700; accrual duration: 25.33; final analysis at: 58.66
#>   Power: 0.9001
#>   Type I error: 0.025 (non-binding), 0.02482 (binding)
#>  look  time events info_frac z_upper  p_upper hr_upper z_lower hr_lower
#>     1 25.45    294      0.50   2.963 0.001525   0.7078 -0.5039   1.0605
#>     2 35.51    441      0.75   2.359 0.009162   0.7988  0.7166   0.9340
#>     3 58.66    588      1.00   2.014 0.022000   0.8469  2.0141   0.8469
#>  prob_upper prob_lower cum_power
#>     0.06203    0.02689   0.06203
#>     0.46398    0.02760   0.52601
#>     0.37413    0.04536   0.90014

The accrual ends at month 25.3. The final analysis needs 588 events and takes place at month 58.7. The type I error is 0.025 when the futility bounds are ignored.

The mean of the standardized statistic can be computed directly from the hazards (default) or with the Schoenfeld approximation, which uses the event-weighted average of the log hazard ratio.

t_fin <- des$study_duration
rbind(direct = lr_moments(scn, 700, t_fin)$z_mean,
      schoenfeld = lr_moments(scn, 700, t_fin, mean = "schoenfeld")$z_mean)
#>                [,1]
#> direct     3.395909
#> schoenfeld 3.417165

Overall survival with switching after progression

In the control group the hazard of progression is 0.10 per month in the first 4 months and 0.08 afterwards. At progression, 30 percent of the patients switch to the experimental treatment; the others may switch later with a hazard of 0.04 per month. After progression the hazard of death is 0.06 without switch and 0.035 after a switch. The treatment group has a lower hazard of progression and no switching.

ctl_sw <- ms_model(time = c(0, 4), prog = c(0.10, 0.08), death = 0.01,
                   switch_prob = 0.3, death_prog = 0.06, switch_rate = 0.04,
                   death_switch = 0.035, dropout = 0.003)
trt_sw <- ms_model(time = c(0, 4), prog = c(0.06, 0.05), death = 0.008,
                   death_prog = 0.055, dropout = 0.003)
ms_prob(ctl_sw, time = c(6, 12, 24))
#>   time progression_free progressed  switched      dead
#> 1    6        0.5379444  0.2102858 0.1417831 0.1099867
#> 2   12        0.3134862  0.2176410 0.2161661 0.2527068
#> 3   24        0.1064585  0.1329666 0.2539857 0.5065892

The post-progression intensities are measured from the time of progression (clock = "reset", the default). OS and progression-free survival (PFS) of the control group at 12 months are 0.747 and 0.313.

scn_sw <- ms_scenario(ctl_sw, trt_sw, accrual = ms_accrual(rate = 25))
pw <- ms_power(scn_sw, n = 500, looks = ms_looks("os", fraction = c(0.6, 1)),
               test = ms_test(), events = 300)
pw
#> Group sequential log-rank design
#>   Tested endpoint: OS; looks driven by OS events
#>   Sample size: 500; accrual duration: 20; final analysis at: 43.89
#>   Power: 0.2206
#>   Type I error: 0.025 (non-binding), 0.025 (binding)
#>  look  time events info_frac z_upper  p_upper hr_upper z_lower hr_lower
#>     1 28.82    180       0.6   2.669 0.003808   0.6718    -Inf       NA
#>     2 43.89    300       1.0   1.981 0.023798   0.7955   1.981   0.7955
#>  prob_upper prob_lower cum_power
#>     0.08221     0.0000   0.08221
#>     0.13839     0.7794   0.22059

With 300 OS events the power is 0.221. Switching to the experimental treatment in the control group moves the hazard ratio for OS towards 1. For comparison, the same design without switching (all switching intensities set to zero) has the power

ctl_ns <- ms_model(time = c(0, 4), prog = c(0.10, 0.08), death = 0.01,
                   death_prog = 0.06, dropout = 0.003)
scn_ns <- ms_scenario(ctl_ns, trt_sw, accrual = ms_accrual(rate = 25))
pw_ns <- ms_power(scn_ns, n = 500, looks = ms_looks("os", fraction = c(0.6, 1)),
                  test = ms_test(), events = 300)
pw_ns$power
#> [1] 0.8426871

PFS and OS tested together

Both groups follow the model of Fleischer et al. (2009): the times to progression and to death are exponential and the hazard of death does not change at progression, so that PFS and OS are exponential. The medians of PFS and OS are 4 and 12 months in the control group and 6 and 16 months in the treatment group, and patients are enrolled at 25 per month.

PFS is tested at 300 PFS events, where OS is also tested, and OS is tested again at 220 OS events. With the fixed-sequence procedure, both hypotheses are tested at level 0.025 and OS is tested only after PFS has been rejected (procedure (b) of Glimm et al. 2010). Each endpoint has its own efficacy bounds of O’Brien-Fleming type.

fl <- ms_scenario(ms_fleischer(median_pfs = 4, median_os = 12),
                  ms_fleischer(median_pfs = 6, median_os = 16),
                  accrual = ms_accrual(rate = 25))
lk2 <- ms_looks(c("pfs", "os"), fraction = c(1, 1),
                test = list(c("pfs", "os"), "os"))
fs <- ms_power(fl, n = 450, looks = lk2,
               test = ms_test(endpoints = c("pfs", "os"), mtp = "fixed_sequence"),
               events = c(pfs = 300, os = 220))
fs
#> Group sequential log-rank design with two endpoints
#>   Endpoints: PFS, then OS (fixed sequence, overall); looks driven by PFS events and OS events
#>   Sample size: 450; accrual duration: 18; final analysis at: 23.05
#>   Power: PFS 0.9387, OS 0.5452; both 0.5452; at least one 0.9387
#>   FWER under global null: 0.025 (non-binding), 0.025 (binding)
#>  endpoint look  time events info_frac z_upper  p_upper hr_upper z_lower
#>       PFS    1 18.62    300    1.0000   1.960 0.025000   0.7975   1.960
#>        OS    1 18.62    163    0.7407   2.357 0.009207   0.6912    -Inf
#>        OS    2 23.05    220    1.0000   2.009 0.022243   0.7626   2.009
#>  hr_lower prob_upper prob_lower cum_power
#>    0.7975     0.9387          0    0.9387
#>        NA     0.2966          0    0.2966
#>    0.7626     0.2486          0    0.5452

The power is 0.939 for PFS and 0.545 for OS, and both hypotheses are rejected with probability 0.545. The final OS analysis takes place at month 23.1.

The Bonferroni procedure tests PFS at level 0.02 and OS at level 0.005, whatever happens to the other hypothesis.

bf <- ms_power(fl, n = 450, looks = lk2,
               test = ms_test(endpoints = c("pfs", "os"), mtp = "bonferroni",
                              weights = c(0.8, 0.2)),
               events = c(pfs = 300, os = 220))
rbind(fixed_sequence = fs$power, bonferroni = bf$power)
#>                      pfs        os      both       any
#> fixed_sequence 0.9387378 0.5451639 0.5451639 0.9387378
#> bonferroni     0.9265375 0.3237669 0.3173922 0.9329122

The familywise error rate is computed under the global null hypothesis, where the correlation between the PFS and OS statistics is that of Danzer et al. (2025). A partial null hypothesis, in which OS is the same in both groups but PFS is not, can be given through null_scenarios:

os_null <- ms_scenario(ms_fleischer(median_pfs = 4, median_os = 12),
                       ms_fleischer(median_pfs = 6, median_os = 12),
                       accrual = ms_accrual(rate = 25))
ms_power(fl, n = 450, looks = lk2,
         test = ms_test(endpoints = c("pfs", "os"), mtp = "fixed_sequence"),
         events = c(pfs = 300, os = 220), null_scenarios = list(os = os_null))$fwer
#>              scenario null_endpoints nonbinding    binding
#> 1              global        PFS, OS 0.02500000 0.02500000
#> 2 null_scenarios[[1]]             OS 0.02405394 0.02405394

Choice of the covariance

The argument variance of ms_test() (and of lr_moments() and lr_cov()) chooses the covariance of the standardized statistics. By default ("null") the statistics of one endpoint have unit variances and the correlations of independent increments. With "alternative", the variance and covariance of the score under the alternative hypothesis (Luo et al. 2019) are used instead. With "studentized", the covariance is the asymptotic covariance of the statistic that is computed in practice, standardized by the estimated variance and, for event-driven analyses, taken at a random analysis time.

mo <- lapply(c(alternative = "alternative", studentized = "studentized"),
             function(v) lr_moments(scn, n = 700, calendar_time = c(24, t_fin),
                                    variance = v))
sapply(mo, function(m) m$z_var)
#>      alternative studentized
#> [1,]   0.9985616   1.0004021
#> [2,]   0.9530797   0.9900072

Here the largest difference of the variances from 1 is 0.047 with "alternative" and 0.01 with "studentized". The choice affects the power and the futility bounds by beta spending, but not the efficacy bounds or the non-binding type I error. In the simulations of inst/validation/ with PFS and OS tested together, "studentized" agreed best with the simulated standard deviations and correlations of the statistics, and the powers with "null" and "studentized" agreed with the simulated powers within the Monte Carlo error.

References

Danzer MF, Rufibach K, Beyersmann J, Schmidt R (2025). Exhausting the type I error level in event-driven group-sequential designs with a closed testing procedure for progression-free and overall survival. arXiv:2512.08658.

Fleischer F, Gaschler-Markefski B, Bluhmki E (2009). A statistical model for the dependence between progression-free survival and overall survival. Statistics in Medicine 28:2669-2686.

Glimm E, Maurer W, Bretz F (2010). Hierarchical testing of multiple endpoints in group-sequential trials. Statistics in Medicine 29:219-228.

Luo X, Mao X, Chen X, Qiu J, Bai S, Quan H (2019). Design and monitoring of survival trials in complex scenarios. Statistics in Medicine 38:192-209.
